title: Anesthetic management for pulsed field ablation in a patient with Eisenmenger syndrome using general anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation: a case report
summary: Abstract Background Drug-refractory atrial tachyarrhythmia is an important precipitating factor for recurrent heart failure decompensation in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome (ES). Although percutaneous pulsed field ablation (PFA) represents a potential therapeutic option for arrhythmia management, its application in this population is challenging due to the substantial anesthetic risks associated with severe pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular dysfunction, and profound hypoxemia. Case presentation We report the case of a 48-year-old male with ES and chronic heart failure who presented with recurrent, drug-refractory atrial flutter/fibrillation. Given concerns regarding hemodynamic deterioration during positive pressure ventilation, general anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation supported by a laryngeal mask airway was selected. The PFA was successfully completed without intraoperative hemodynamic instability. The patient was transferred to the ward with supplemental oxygen support. However, despite successful arrhythmia ablation and favorable intraprocedural physiology, he developed progressive heart failure and multiorgan dysfunction and died 20 days after the procedure. Conclusion The safe implementation of PFA relies on absolute immobility and stable hemodynamics. An anesthesia strategy utilizing general anesthesia with a laryngeal mask airway and spontaneous ventilation avoids the deleterious effects of positive intrathoracic pressure on right ventricular preload, allowing the PFA procedure to be completed with stable physiology and acute rhythm control.

title: Trends and disparities in mortality involving aortic stenosis and atrial fibrillation among United States adults aged ≥ 55 years: a 26-year CDC WONDER analysis (1999–2024)
summary: Abstract Introduction Aortic stenosis (AS) and atrial fibrillation (AF) frequently coexist in older adults and are associated with increased cardiovascular risk. National mortality trends involving both conditions remain incompletely characterized. Methods We performed a nationwide ecological time-trend analysis using the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database from 1999 to 2024. Adults aged ≥ 55 years with both AS (ICD-10 I35.0) and AF (ICD-10 I48) listed on the death certificate were included. Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) per 100,000 populations were analyzed overall and by sex, race/ethnicity, census region, urbanization, and place of death. Temporal trends were assessed using Joinpoint regression. Results A total of 94,542 deaths involving AS and AF were identified. Overall AAMR increased from 2.4 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.3–2.6) in 1999 to 7.4 (95% CI, 7.2–7.6) in 2024, with a significant overall increase (average annual percent change [AAPC], 5.08%; p < 0.001). Mortality remained higher among males than females (2024 AAMR: 9.2 vs. 6.1 per 100,000). NH White individuals had the highest mortality rates, while all racial and ethnic groups demonstrated significant increases over time. Mortality was highest in the Western United States and in non-metropolitan areas. Most deaths occurred in inpatient facilities (33.8%), followed by home (29.0%) and nursing homes or long-term care facilities (22.6%). Conclusion Mortality involving coexisting AS and AF increased more than threefold among U.S. adults aged ≥ 55 years between 1999 and 2024. Persistent demographic and geographic disparities highlight the need for earlier diagnosis and improved access to guideline-directed care. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: When a Lung Collapses: A Case of Polymicrobial Empyema Presenting as Massive Hydropneumothorax.
summary: Aspiration-related pneumonia can progress to empyema and massive hydropneumothorax, potentially fatal complications not frequently documented in the literature. Patients with structural lung disease and poor dentition can be particularly vulnerable to severe polymicrobial infections arising from seemingly minor aspiration events. We report the case of a man in his early 70s with chronic bronchiectasis, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and poor dentition who presented with progressive dyspnea and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Imaging demonstrated a massive right-sided hydropneumothorax with complete right lung collapse and mediastinal shift. Pleural fluid cultures grew Streptococcus anginosus and Prevotella nigrescens, consistent with aspiration-related polymicrobial empyema. His hospital course was complicated by septic shock requiring vasopressor support, atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response requiring synchronized cardioversion, and pulseless ventricular tachycardia with successful return of spontaneous circulation. Management included chest tube drainage, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics followed by de-escalation, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and multidisciplinary critical care support. Despite severe multiorgan compromise, the patient ultimately improved and was discharged home on prolonged oral antibiotic therapy. This case illustrates how a seemingly simple aspiration event can progress into catastrophic pleuropulmonary disease with life-threatening cardiopulmonary collapse. Early recognition, prompt source control, and multidisciplinary management were critical to improving the outcome for this patient.

title: Measuring a moving target: analytic considerations for atrial fibrillation density
Atrial fibrillation density and stroke risk: a promising advance that now needs predictive validation
LAA occluder device impeding pulsed field ablation of an anterior mitral line: a case report about the role of a dual energy source
summary: Background Pulsed field ablation (PFA) and percutaneous closure of the left atrial appendage are increasingly used in patients with atrial fibrillation. An interaction between this form of energy and metallic structures in the heart is an emerging problem. We first report a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC)-limiting PFA using a novel dual energy ablation catheter, solved by switching to the classic radiofrequency ablation.Case summary An 85-year-old woman with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and a history of persistent atrial fibrillation (status post pulmonary vein isolation in 2019, with a 25 mm Abbott Amulet LAAC implanted in 2023) presented with recurrent atrial tachycardia. During redo ablation, mapping revealed a macroreentrant circuit through an anterior left atrial low-voltage area. While extending a linear PFA lesion towards the LAAC, the generator repeatedly aborted applications due to invalid impedance values near the device-despite the device having been in place for 3 years. Switching to radiofrequency energy on the same catheter allowed the line to be completed successfully, achieving bidirectional block and tachycardia non-inducibility.Discussion The interaction between PFA and metallic cardiac devices may limit catheter ablation, a problem that can be solved by technologies that allow for the switch to radiofrequency sources. Dual energy technologies may be therefore preferred in patients with LAAC devices.

title: Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: The CHAMPION-like vs CLOSURE-like Patient Phenotype Framework.
summary:
AIMS: The near-simultaneous publication of CHAMPION-AF and CLOSURE-AF produced apparently discordant evidence regarding percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. We aimed to reconcile these findings through a phenotype-based framework and identify the determinants of net clinical benefit.

METHODS AND RESULTS: This narrative review integrates randomized trials, registries, consensus documents, and guidelines, focusing on patient selection, procedural risk, post-implant antithrombotic therapy, endpoint construction, competing mortality, and time to benefit. CHAMPION-AF evaluated LAAC against direct oral anticoagulation in an elective, anticoagulation-eligible population with lower bleeding risk, demonstrating non-inferior thromboembolic protection and less non-procedural bleeding. Conversely, CLOSURE-AF enrolled an older, multimorbid population with substantial renal dysfunction, previous bleeding, and high competing mortality. Although implantation success and stroke rates were comparable between treatment groups, early procedural and antithrombotic-related bleeding, a composite endpoint incorporating procedural events, and limited survival reduced the opportunity for delayed benefit. The highly selective recruitment pathway further limits generalisability. These findings define a continuum from the "CHAMPION-like" patient, with sufficient physiological reserve and life expectancy to realise long-term benefit, to the "CLOSURE-like" patient, in whom frailty and competing risk may outweigh the advantage of appendage exclusion.

CONCLUSION: LAAC efficacy is not determined by device performance alone but by matching the intervention to patient phenotype and time horizon. Selection should integrate thromboembolic and bleeding risk, frailty, renal function, post-implant treatment tolerance, and expected survival. Future trials require transparent screening data, time-sensitive endpoints, landmark analyses, and competing-risk methods.

title: Efficacy, safety, and strategy-modifying factors of pulsed field ablation for persistent and long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
summary: Background Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is increasingly applied in persistent atrial fibrillation (PerAF) and long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation (LSPAF). Previous reviews of mixed AF populations suggested potential advantages in procedural efficiency and esophageal safety, but PerAF/LSPAF-specific evidence on long-term rhythm outcomes and on the value of posterior wall or extended substrate strategies remains limited, with substantial heterogeneity in lesion sets, endpoint definitions, and comparator types.Methods We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Scopus through April 18, 2026, with an updated verification search performed in August 2026. Because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity, formal pairwise pooling was restricted to comparisons supported by at least two clinically homogeneous head-to-head studies; single-study comparisons were synthesized narratively, and strategy-level outcomes were explored with single-arm proportion meta-analysis of exact-count cohorts. Off-antiarrhythmic drug (off-AAD) outcomes were prioritized when available. Certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE approach.Results Twenty-two studies (approximately 3,100 patients) were included. In an exploratory pooled analysis of the only two available head-to-head comparisons (380 patients, with imbalanced study weights and different lesion sets: PVI-only vs. PVI plus posterior wall isolation), PFA was associated with lower 12-month atrial arrhythmia recurrence than cryoballoon ablation [risk ratio [RR] 0.71, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51-0.98; GRADE certainty: very low]; this is best regarded as a preliminary signal. No statistically detectable difference in major complications was observed between PFA and cryoballoon [risk difference (RD) 0.00, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.02], reflecting absence of a demonstrable difference rather than proven equivalence. Single-study comparisons against radiofrequency ablation (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45-0.94) and hybrid-convergent ablation (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.67-1.86) yielded directionally discordant results and are presented narratively. Exploratory, non-comparative single-arm analyses yielded pooled 12-month freedom from atrial arrhythmia of 66.0% (95% CI 55.5%-75.2%; I²=79.0%) for PVI plus posterior wall cohorts and 82.6% (95% CI 76.3%-87.5%; I 2 = 0%) for beyond-PV/extended substrate cohorts; these estimates derive from different, non-randomized cohorts and are hypothesis-generating only.Conclusions Current evidence suggests favorable efficacy and safety of PFA in PerAF/LSPAF, but certainty is low to very low for all key outcomes. The lower recurrence vs. cryoballoon ablation is an encouraging but preliminary signal requiring confirmation in adequately powered randomized trials with uniform lesion sets. Whether extended substrate strategies improve outcomes cannot be determined from current non-comparative data. Future studies should apply standardized off-AAD endpoints, uniform rhythm monitoring, and stratification by atrial myopathy burden and PFA platform.Systematic review registration identifier INPLASY202640082; doi: 10.37766/inplasy2026.4.0082.

title: Single versus double transseptal puncture for atrial fibrillation radiofrequency ablation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
summary: Background The single puncture technique has emerged as an alternative to conventional double transseptal puncture for radiofrequency ablation of atrial fibrillation (AF). This meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of these two approaches.Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library up to 1st March, 2026. Prospective and retrospective cohort studies comparing single vs. double transseptal puncture during AF ablation were included. The primary outcome was the sinus rhythm maintenance. Secondary outcomes included total procedure time, fluoroscopy time, and periprocedural complications. Data were pooled using a random-effects model, and heterogeneity was assessed with the I² statistic.Results Four studies involving 1811 patients were included. No significant difference was observed in 3-month sinus rhythm maintenance between the single- and double-puncture groups (OR 1.20, 95% CI: 0.95-1.51, P = 0.13). While fluoroscopy time presented similar values (MD -0.84, 95% CI: -4.80-3.11, P = 0.68), procedure duration was significantly longer with single transseptal puncture (MD 11.65, 95% CI: 2.62-20.69, P = 0.01). The incidence of periprocedural complications was similar between the two strategies (OR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.47-1.38, P = 0.43).Conclusions Single transseptal puncture represents an effective and safe alternative to double puncture for atrial fibrillation ablation, with comparable rhythm outcomes, fluoroscopy exposure and complication rates, despite longer procedural duration.Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/view/CRD420261300869, Identifier: CRD420261300869.

title: Case Report: Angiography-guided transvenous single-chamber pacemaker implantation in mirror-image dextrocardia with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries
summary: Background Mirror-image dextrocardia with situs inversus is uncommon. Transvenous permanent pacemaker implantation is technically demanding when it coexists with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA), because venous access, atrioventricular valve crossing, and fluoroscopic lead orientation may differ from usual anatomy.Case presentation A 61-year-old man was admitted with recurrent dizziness and palpitations for 5 years; his symptoms had worsened during the preceding 2 weeks. Preoperative 12-lead electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring documented 707 pauses longer than 2.0 s, with a longest R-R interval of 6.13 s. Echocardiography confirmed mirror-image dextrocardia, situs inversus, and ccTGA. A single-chamber permanent pacemaker was implanted through the right axillary vein. Posteroanterior fluoroscopy defined the right-sided cardiac silhouette; right axillary venography guided venous puncture; right atrial angiography identified the morphologic mitral annular plane; and multi-projection fluoroscopy was used to confirm the final ventricular lead position in the high mid-septal region of the morphologic left ventricle. The procedure lasted 56 min and had no acute complications. At 6-month outpatient follow-up, standard 12-lead electrocardiography, 24-hour Holter monitoring, formal device interrogation, and transthoracic echocardiography showed stable pacing, preserved ventricular performance, and no device-related complication; the paced QRS duration was 144 ms and the pacing burden was 99.8%. During telephone follow-up in June 2026, approximately 1 year after implantation, the patient reported no discomfort.Conclusion This case describes a structured approach to conventional transvenous pacemaker implantation in mirror-image dextrocardia with ccTGA. In this patient, venography, chamber angiography, and targeted fluoroscopic views reduced procedural uncertainty, and follow-up through 1 year showed clinical stability without recognized complications.

title: Maintenance of atrial fibrillation by reciprocal triggering of competitive focal sources: a hypothesis
summary: The primary mechanism of atrial fibrillation (AF) maintenance remains debatable. However, contemporary atrial surface AF mapping studies readily detect multifocal activity, less readily "incomplete reentries" (defining them as reentries or false reentries) and never or rarely full-circuit reentries. Most of the surface multifocal waves during AF are short-lasting (1-3 waves) and they appear to be largely breakthroughs. Some of the multifocal activities during AF, particularly repetitive/sustained, can be explained with reciprocal triggering of delayed afterdepolarization (DAD) activities. Indeed, the condition that causes DAD activity (i.e., intracellular calcium abnormalities plus rapid activation) is continuously present during AF throughout the atria, that may provide a sufficient "arrhythmogenic reserve" for the generation of multiple competitive focal sources sustaining AF. In such scenario, there should be commonly one dominant source at a time along with subsidiary active and/or latent/overridden sources (the currently fastest sustained source acts to override all the others, covering all, most, or a large part of the atrium at a time). This may account for a spatiotemporal periodicity usually recorded during AF. Sustained focal sources should self-terminate/decelerate sooner or later and/or be overridden by currently faster sources, entailing a periodical switching of dominant sources (the currently "fittest" dominates). Anti-AF success of the Cox-Maze and pulmonary vein isolation procedures, separating the main atrial arrhythmogenic regions, can be generally explained with the interruption of mutual triggering of multiple DAD sources. Thus, reciprocal triggering of competitive DAD sources may broadly account for the maintenance and spatiotemporal periodicity of AF as well as for the anti-AF success of the Cox-Maze and pulmonary vein isolation procedures.

title: One-year outcomes in patients with persistent atrial fibrillation using CARTOFINDER mapping with OCTARAY: a Shinshu-AB registry study.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Persistent atrial fibrillation (PerAF) has no established method of catheter ablation. Although catheter ablation using CARTOFINDER has shown some therapeutic effects, the associated prolonged procedure time remains a challenge. The identification of focal or rotational activation sites by CARTOFINDER using OCTARAY™ Mapping Catheter (OCTARAY) suggests that it can more efficiently detect the activation sites owing to its greater coverage of the left atrium (LA). This study aimed to compare the outcomes of catheter ablation guided by CARTOFINDER versus BOX isolation (BOXI) in patients with PerAF.

METHODS: Using the Shinshu-AB registry, the study included 117 patients with PerAF who underwent catheter ablation between May 2021 and May 2024. The patients were matched at 1:1 ratio (n = 39 each): Group 1 underwent CARTOFINDER-guided catheter ablation, and Group 2 underwent BOXI-guided catheter ablation. CARTOFINDER detection was limited to four sites on the LA posterior wall, the LA appendage ostium, and the LA septum, for a total of six sites.

RESULTS: Procedure time was significantly shorter in Group 1 (140.2 ± 37.7 vs. 174.4 ± 74.1 min, p = 0.016). The 1-year AF recurrence rate was significantly lower in Group 1 (17.9% vs. 38.5%, p = 0.031). Based on Cox proportional hazards regression analysis, AF duration and CARTOFINDER-guided catheter ablation were both independent predictors of recurrent AF after catheter ablation for PerAF.

CONCLUSION: Compared to BOXI, CARTOFINDER-guided catheter ablation may lead to better outcomes in patients with PerAF.

title: Molecular phenotyping of atrial remodeling in atrial fibrillation using 18F-FDG and 18F-FAPI PET.
summary: Atrial remodeling in atrial fibrillation (AF) involves multiple biological processes, including metabolic alterations, inflammation-related metabolic activity, and fibroblast activation, which can be assessed non-invasively with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) and fibroblast activation protein inhibitors (FAPI) PET, respectively. We aimed to characterize and compare the atrial uptake patterns of these two tracers in patients with AF. In this post hoc cardinality-matched analysis of two prospective PET/CT cohorts, 90 patients with AF were included (45 imaged with ¹⁸F-FDG and 45 with ¹⁸F-FAPI). Left atrial volume index (LAVI) was measured using the echocardiographic ellipsoid method. The prevalence, intensity, and spatial distribution of atrial tracer uptake were compared between tracers, and clinical correlates of abnormal uptake were assessed using univariable analyses and logistic regression. ¹⁸F-FAPI showed a higher left atrial (LA) target-to-background ratio than ¹⁸F-FDG (P = 0.007). Abnormal uptake was more frequent with ¹⁸F-FDG in the left atrial appendage (LAA; 83.3% vs. 23.1%, P < 0.001), and more frequent with ¹⁸F-FAPI in the LA anterior wall (84.6% vs. 38.9%, P = 0.002) and LA roof (69.2% vs. 33.3%, P = 0.019). These differences persisted in persistent AF (PsAF); in paroxysmal AF, only the higher LAA ¹⁸F-FDG uptake remained (P = 0.015). Abnormal right atrial ¹⁸F-FDG uptake was associated with PsAF (P = 0.010), whereas abnormal LA ¹⁸F-FAPI uptake was associated with higher LAVI (P = 0.021) and lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (P = 0.006). ¹⁸F-FDG and ¹⁸F-FAPI PET demonstrated spatially divergent atrial uptake patterns in AF, suggesting cohort-level complementary information on metabolically active atrial remodeling and activated fibroblast-associated remodeling. This complementarity requires within-patient validation.

title: Colchicine for Prevention of Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Clinical Implications.
summary: Cardiovascular disease represents the foremost cause of mortality globally. Annually, there are approximately 720,000 new cases of myocardial infarction and 335,000 recurrent events. Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) continues to be a primary intervention for multivessel coronary artery disease, using venous or arterial conduits to circumvent obstructed coronary vessels. In the United States, approximately 200,000 CABG procedures are conducted each year. Compared with percutaneous coronary intervention, CABG is favored in patients with advanced atherosclerosis, diabetes, and complex coronary anatomy. Despite advancements in surgical techniques and perioperative care, CABG continues to be associated with significant complications, including infection, stroke, renal failure, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pleural effusion, arrhythmias, prolonged ventilatory support, myocardial infarction, post-pericardiotomy syndrome, and delirium. The occurrence of these complications is contingent on pre-existing risk factors as well as intraoperative and postoperative variables. One significant postoperative complication is atrial fibrillation, which affects 16% to 50% of patients and typically manifests 2 to 4 days following surgery. Colchicine, an anti-inflammatory agent traditionally used in the treatment of gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, has emerged as a potential therapeutic option for mitigating inflammation-associated complications, such as postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF). This review investigates the role of colchicine in the prevention of POAF following CABG, analyzing proposed mechanisms, relevant clinical trials, and potential clinical implications.

title: Systolic Blood Pressure Variability and Outcomes in Atrial Fibrillation: A Nationwide Population Study in Korea
summary: Background The relationship between systolic blood pressure variability (SBP-V) and clinical outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) remains unclear.Methods Using the Korean National Health Insurance database, we included patients with prevalent AF who received health checkups in 2013-2014, with at least three checkups in total (n = 235,091). SBP-V was defined as the standard deviation of SBP. The outcomes, including stroke, major bleeding, and all-cause death, were assessed during follow-up.Results During the follow-up period (median, 4.9 years; interquartile range, 4.3-5.3), 5,339 strokes (0.5/100 person-years [PYs]), 3,432 major bleeding incidents (0.3/100 PYs), and 16,755 all-cause mortality (1.5/100 PYs) occurred. Compared to patients with SBP 120 to < 130 mmHg at the index health checkup, those with SBP ≥ 130 mmHg had a significantly higher risks of stroke and major bleeding. All-cause mortality was elevated at both high (≥ 150 mmHg) and low (< 120 mmHg) SBP levels. Compared to the lowest SBP-V group, the highest SBP-V group had significantly higher risks of stroke (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.211; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.125-1.304), major bleeding (aHR, 1.125; 95% CI, 1.025-1.234), and all-cause death (aHR, 1.189; 95% CI, 1.141-1.239). No significant interactions were observed between oral anticoagulation use and SBP-V for any of the clinical outcomes.Conclusion SBP and SBP-V were independently associated with higher risks of stroke, major bleeding, and all-cause death in patients with AF. These findings highlight the importance of not only achieving target blood pressure levels but also minimizing SBP variability through optimal hypertension management to improve outcomes in this population.

title: CoBiDiff: Anatomy-aware bidirectional diffusion for left atrium cross-modal augmentation
summary: Abstract Accurate delineation of the left atrium (LA) from cardiac magnetic resonance (MR) and computed tomography (CT) images plays an important role in atrial fibrillation (AF) assessment and treatment planning. However, the limited availability of expert-annotated cardiac datasets restricts the robustness and generalizability of deep learning–based segmentation models, particularly in cross-modal scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we propose CoBiDiff, a collaborative bidirectional diffusion framework that explicitly incorporates anatomical constraints into unpaired cross-modal cardiac image augmentation. The framework is developed using unpaired CT and MR volumes from the MICCAI 2017 Multi-Modality Whole Heart Segmentation (MM-WHS) challenge dataset, focusing specifically on the LA region. A shared diffusion backbone is employed to jointly model both imaging modalities, while signed distance functions (SDFs) are incorporated as structural representations to provide anatomical guidance during generation. To reduce the influence of artificial CT field-of-view (FOV) boundaries, boundary regions are suppressed through noise replacement and gradient smoothing strategies. In addition, a soft spatial extent loss is introduced to maintain anatomically plausible foreground spatial extents during synthesis. An SDF dropout strategy is further introduced during training to strengthen image-conditioned anatomical inference and improve anatomical coherence. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework generates LA images with improved structural consistency across modalities. The proposed method achieved Dice coefficients (DCs) of 86.53% and 95.04%, and average symmetric surface distances (ASSDs) of 1.511 mm and 0.623 mm for CT-to-MR and MR-to-CT augmentation, respectively, on the MM-WHS 2017 dataset. CoBiDiff provides a practical framework for expanding limited cardiac imaging datasets without requiring paired cross-modal images. By combining diffusion-based synthesis with anatomy-aware constraints, CoBiDiff improves the downstream utility of generated samples for cardiac segmentation. The full implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/PencilSC/CoBiDiff to support reproducible and open research.

title: Population Mortality Involving Co-Reported Intracerebral Hemorrhage and Atrial Fibrillation or Flutter in the United States, 1999-2025: Trends, Demographic Disparities, and Forecasts to 2040.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Atrial fibrillation (AF) increases the risk of anticoagulation-associated intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), yet contemporary national mortality trends specific to this overlap remain undercharacterized. Temporal, demographic, and geographic trends in ICH mortality among patients with concomitant AF in the United States from 1999 to 2025, with projections to 2040, were examined.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis of death certificate data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) database was conducted, identifying deaths listing ICH (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] code I61) and AF (ICD-10 code I48) in any cause-of-death field. Age-adjusted mortality rates were calculated per 100,000 population and stratified by sex, race/ethnicity, census region, and urbanization. Joinpoint regression assessed temporal trends, and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models projected rates through 2040.

RESULTS: From 1999 to 2025, 52,967 deaths were identified. The overall age-adjusted mortality rate rose from 0.4 to 0.7 per 100,000 between 1999 and 2021 (annual percent change [APC] 1.53%, p=0.016) before stabilizing through 2025. Mortality was consistently higher among men and rose significantly across the study period among Black or African American individuals (APC 1.83%, p<0.000001). Nonmetropolitan areas and the West and South regions carried the highest burden, while the Northeast declined after 2015. State rates ranged from 0.3 in Louisiana to 1.1 in Vermont, and most deaths occurred in medical facilities.

CONCLUSIONS: Mortality from ICH among patients with AF rose substantially before stabilizing, with persistent disparities by sex, race, and geography. Projections through 2040 indicate stable rates but a growing absolute burden, underscoring the need for equitable hypertension control and anticoagulation management.

title: Antiplatelet or Anticoagulant Therapy in Cardiac Patients Undergoing Dental Procedures: A Systematic Review of Clinical Practice Guidelines and Consensus Recommendations
summary: Large numbers of patients with coronary artery disease, prior myocardial infarction, coronary stents, atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism or prosthetic heart valves take antiplatelet agents (for example aspirin, clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) or anticoagulants (vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin and acenocoumarol, and direct oral anticoagulants such as dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban). These patients frequently need dental extractions, minor oral surgery and other invasive dental procedures. Dentists face two competing risks. Continuing therapy may increase local bleeding, which is usually manageable with local haemostatic measures. Interrupting or modifying therapy may expose the patient to stent thrombosis, stroke or systemic thromboembolism, which can be catastrophic. Recommendations on whether to continue, interrupt, bridge or adjust therapy, on peri-procedural INR thresholds, and on the timing of DOAC doses vary between cardiology, haematology, oral surgery and dental guidelines. They are also updated at different times, and older guidance still circulates in practice. A structured synthesis of what the guidelines recommend, how consistent they are, and how rigorously they were developed would help clinicians and guideline developers identify areas of agreement and conflict. We found no recent systematic review that appraises and compares guidelines specifically for cardiac patients on antithrombotic therapy undergoing dental treatment.

title: Management strategies for new-onset AF after cardiac surgery in patients with low ejection fraction: a scoping review
summary: Management strategies for new-onset AF after cardiac surgery in patients with low ejection fraction: a scoping review 1. Background and rationale New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) is the most common arrhythmic complication after cardiac surgery. Patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) are a distinct and under-studied subgroup. The limited contractile reserve and frequent dependence on inotropic support following cardiac surgery make these patients especially vulnerable to the haemodynamic consequences of NOAF and to the adverse effects of the drugs commonly used to treat it. The rationale for focusing on this population is fourfold: 1. Because of low EF and the inherent potential for haemodynamic instability, these patients are a less-studied segment and are frequently excluded from, or under-represented in, trials of AF management. 2. The drugs most frequently used for acute AF management — beta-blockers and amiodarone — both carry potential for significant negative inotropic effects. 3. Restarting beta-blockers in patients with low EF previously on chronic beta-blocker treatment is contraindicated if there is concurrent inotrope support needed. 4. Patients with reduced systolic function frequently need inotrope treatment in the immediate aftermath of cardiac surgery, which are known to trigger cardiac arrhythmias, including AF. This scoping review is intended to map current practice, recommendations and the underlying evidence for managing NOAF after cardiac surgery in patients with low EF. Its findings will inform future research into optimal pharmacological options. Whether an ultra-short-acting, highly cardioselective beta-blocker such as landiolol could address the identified gap is a motivating question for this review, but is not a hypothesis this scoping review sets out to test. 2. Review question and objectives Review question: What is the current practice for the management of new-onset AF after cardiac surgery in adult patients with low ejection fraction, and what is the evidence supporting it? Objectives: • pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies used to manage NOAF in this population (rate control, rhythm control, cardioversion); • clinical outcomes reported against those strategies; • existing guidelines and recommendations relevant to this subgroup; • evidence gaps — in particular the extent to which low-EF patients are represented in the available literature. 3. Eligibility criteria Population (P): Adults (≥18 y) undergoing cardiac surgery (CABG, valve, combined, aortic) with reduced/impaired left ventricular function — LVEF < 40% (HFrEF / LV systolic dysfunction) Concept (C): Management strategies for new-onset (post-operative) atrial fibrillation — pharmacological and non-pharmacological — and the outcomes associated with them Context (C): Postoperative adult cardiac ICU; any country or health system Inclusion criteria: • Adult patients (≥18 years). • No past medical history of long-standing or permanent AF, and no prior electrophysiological treatment for AF. • After cardiac surgery (per definition below), post-operative days 0–7. • Reduced cardiac function: pre-existing LVEF < 40%. • Study designs: RCTs, cohort, case-control, registry and other observational studies. Guidelines, consensus statements and reviews retained for hand-searching and context. Exclusion criteria: • Heart transplantation, ventricular assist device implantation, and surgery for congenital heart disease. • Paediatric populations. • Preserved LV function (LVEF ≥ 40%) 4. Definitions NOAF: New-onset AF in patients without previous history of permanent / long-standing AF, including no history of electrophysiological treatment for AF After cardiac surgery: During the index admission following cardiac surgery, within the first 7 days (days 0–7) Cardiac surgery: Any surgical procedure with sternotomy involving the heart or the pericardium, except transplantation, ventricular assist device implantation, or surgery for congenital heart conditions Low EF: Known preoperative LVEF < 40% Treatments: Drugs and treatment protocols (where available) used to manage NOAF Of note, the interval of 0-7 days was chosen for the following reasons: 1. Highest incidence of NOAF after cardiac surgery. 2. Focus is on patients in intensive care or high-dependency unit (intensive monitoring, likely to need inotropes). 5. Information sources The following will be searched from inception to the search date: • Bibliographic databases: Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL • Citation searching: Web of Science • Grey literature and hand-searching: reference lists of included studies, and relevant guideline bibliographies on postoperative AF. Language: English – for practical purposes and ease of access. 6. Search strategy The strategy uses three core concept blocks combined with AND; within each block, controlled vocabulary (MeSH) is combined with title/abstract/keyword free-text using OR. An optional fourth block (management) is used only to narrow an unmanageable yield. The blocks are summarised in the table below: Block A: New-onset or post-operative atrial fibrillation [Core – Required] Block B: Cardiac surgical procedures [Core – Required] Block C: Left ventricular dysfunction / Systolic heart failure [Core – Required] Block D: Management / Treatment [Optional – Narrowing only] The search will be conducted by combining blocks A AND B AND C, then manually check for D. The strategy will be peer-reviewed against the PRESS 2015 checklist by an information specialist before it is run, and the full run with per-line hit counts and search dates will be recorded for the PRISMA-ScR report. 7. Data charting The following data will be collected using a standardized data-extraction form developed in accordance with the review objectives and relevant PRISMA-ScR guidance. • Study identifiers: Author, year, country, design, setting • Study Population: Sample size, age, sex, surgery type, EF definition & threshold used, baseline comorbidity • AF characteristics: AF definition used, timing/onset, monitoring method, incidence • Intervention / strategy: Drug(s) or non-pharmacological strategy, dose/protocol, timing, rate v. rhythm control, prophylaxis • Comparator: Comparator strategy or none • Outcomes: Outcome domains reported and definitions (see Section 10) • Key findings & gaps: Main results relevant to the review question; author-noted limitations/gaps 8. Outcomes / data items Outcomes will be charted descriptively (no effect estimate). • Rhythm outcomes: conversion to / maintenance of sinus rhythm; AF recurrence; • Rate control achieved; • Haemodynamic outcomes: hypotension, new/increased inotrope or vasopressor requirement, further haemodynamic instability; • Resource use: ICU and total hospital length of stay • Mortality (in-hospital / 30-day) and other reported clinical outcomes; • +/- Thrombotic and/ or bleeding events.

title: Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Pectus Excavatum: Clinical Characteristics, Management, and Outcomes
summary: Background Pectus excavatum (PE), the most common congenital chest wall deformity, has known associations with connective tissue disorders and may lead to cardiopulmonary impairment; however, its relationship with atrial fibrillation (AF) remains underexplored.Objectives This study aimed to describe the frequency, clinical characteristics, and management of AF within an institutional cohort of patients with PE, and to determine whether the outcomes observed in clinically distinct subgroups persisted after adjustment for baseline risk.Methods This was a retrospective cohort study design. Patients with both PE and documented AF between January 1, 1990, and November 10, 2024, were included. Clinical, echocardiographic, and therapeutic data were collected. Bleeding and thromboembolic outcomes were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, CHA2DS2-VASc score, and anticoagulant class, and the surgically treated subgroup was additionally compared using propensity score matching.Results Among 11,578 patients with PE, 1309 (11.3%) had AF. Of those who had AF, mean age was 66.9 years; 54% were female, and 83% had paroxysmal AF. The mean CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores were 2.8 and 1.9, respectively. Thromboembolic events occurred in 196 (15%) patients, most commonly stroke (11%), followed by pulmonary embolism (4%) and deep venous thrombosis (4%). Bleeding events occurred in 313 patients (24%), most commonly hematuria (12%), gastrointestinal bleed (11%), epistaxis (5%), and intracranial hemorrhage (1%). Seventy-two patients (6%) underwent the Nuss procedure and were younger (45.3 vs. 68.2 years, p < 0.001), predominantly male (65%), and had lower risk scores compared to the non-Nuss cohort. Patients who underwent the Nuss procedure had significantly fewer bleeding events (5.6% vs. 25%, p < 0.001) with similar thromboembolic rates. The pectus severity index, available in the 370 patients who underwent dedicated radiologic review, was not associated with bleeding (adjusted OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.75-1.05). The difference in bleeding by surgical status persisted after multivariable adjustment (adjusted OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.10-0.79) and after propensity score matching (5.6% vs. 16.7%, p = 0.030).Conclusions AF was identified in approximately one in nine patients within this single-institution cohort of adults with PE, with paroxysmal AF representing the predominant subtype. Patients who had undergone surgical repair demonstrated a lower incidence of bleeding events than anticipated based on their baseline risk profile; however, given the limited number of events observed, this finding should be interpreted with caution and requires validation in larger studies. In the absence of a non-PE comparator group, these data are insufficient to determine whether PE independently confers an elevated risk of AF, and prospective, controlled investigations are necessary to elucidate this relationship.

title: ACUTE ATRIAL FIBRILLATION: RATE CONTROL WITH BETA-BLOCKERS VERSUS RHYTHM CONTROL WITH ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS
authors: Eberson da Silva Rodrigues do Nascimento
João Guilherme Marques Castello Branco Levy
Luana dos Santos de Jesus Miranda
summary: Acute atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias encountered in emergency care and often requires an early decision between ventricular rate control and restoration of sinus rhythm. This integrative review aimed to synthesize clinical evidence on rate-control strategies with beta-blockers and rhythm-control strategies with antiarrhythmic drugs in adults with acute or recent-onset AF, distinguishing direct comparative evidence from complementary studies addressing efficacy, speed of response, safety, and need for additional interventions. Searches were performed on September 26, 2026, in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus. A total of 700 records were identified (239, 197, and 264, respectively); after 134 duplicates were removed in Rayyan, 566 titles and abstracts were screened, 23 full-text articles were assessed, and 11 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Included studies covered emergency department, intensive care, acute heart failure, and perioperative/anesthesia settings. Intravenous beta-blockers, including esmolol and landiolol, provided rapid ventricular rate reduction in selected settings. In critically ill patients, metoprolol was associated with lower treatment failure, defined by the need for an additional agent, compared with amiodarone. For rhythm control, flecainide and propafenone produced faster pharmacological cardioversion than amiodarone in selected patients without relevant structural heart disease, while early cardioversion strategies achieved high sinus-rhythm restoration rates. However, in haemodynamically stable recent-onset AF, initial rate control and observation allowed frequent spontaneous conversion and similar short-term sinus-rhythm outcomes. No strategy was universally superior; beta-blocker rate control is especially useful for rapid stabilization, whereas rhythm control should be individualized according to AF duration, symptom burden, structural heart disease, ventricular function, haemodynamic status, and thromboembolic safety.

title: Comparative Cardiovascular Physiology in animals- From ECG and Echocardiography to Heart-Organ crosstalk
summary: The cardiovascular system is central to the maintenance of homeostasis, supporting tissue perfusion, oxygen delivery, nutrient transport, thermoregulation and removal of metabolic waste. Although the fundamental principles governing cardiovascular function are conserved across animal species, considerable interspecies variation exists in cardiac anatomy, electrical activity, haemodynamics and responses to physiological and pathological challenges. These differences are particularly evident among companion animals, livestock and wildlife species. Consequently, comparative cardiovascular physiology provides an important framework for understanding normal cardiac function, recognizing disease-associated alterations and identifying species-specific adaptations. In veterinary medicine, cardiovascular assessment has traditionally relied on clinical examination and electrocardiography (ECG), while echocardiography and circulating cardiac biomarkers have progressively expanded the ability to evaluate cardiac structure, function and myocardial injury. The integration of these approaches provides a more comprehensive understanding of cardiovascular health than any single diagnostic modality. ECG as a window into comparative cardiac electrophysiology Electrocardiography remains one of the simplest, rapid and non-invasive methods for assessing cardiac electrical activity. It provides valuable information regarding heart rate, cardiac rhythm, impulse generation and conduction, atrial and ventricular depolarization and repolarization. However, ECG interpretation in animals cannot be completely separated from species, breed, age, body conformation, physiological state and recording conditions. Studies in Labrador Retriever dogs demonstrate that even body position can influence ECG measurements. Dogs examined in right lateral recumbency showed a significantly greater P-wave duration, whereas left lateral positioning was associated with higher T-wave amplitude, QT interval and mean electrical axis. Such findings emphasize that differences in cardiac electrical recordings may not always represent pathology but may partly reflect alterations in cardiac orientation and thoracic geometry associated with body position. Age is another important determinant of the ECG phenotype. In Spitz dogs, progressive age-associated changes were observed in P-wave amplitude, QRS amplitude, heart rate, PR interval, QT interval and several ECG segment durations. Younger dogs exhibited higher heart rates and shorter RR intervals, whereas older dogs showed prolongation of PR and QT intervals. These changes may reflect maturation of the cardiovascular system, age-related alterations in autonomic regulation and changes in myocardial conduction and repolarization. Comparative studies in less frequently investigated species further demonstrate the importance of establishing species-specific reference values. In Indian sloth bears, young animals exhibited higher heart rates and shorter QT intervals than adults, while differences in electrical axis were also evident. Importantly, no clinically significant arrhythmia or cardiac distress was observed following ketamine–xylazine immobilization. Such observations are particularly relevant for wildlife medicine because anaesthesia itself can modify cardiovascular electrophysiology, making species- and age-specific baseline data essential for safe immobilization and clinical interpretation. Physiological states can produce equally striking ECG alterations. Pregnancy, for example, is accompanied by profound cardiovascular adaptation to meet the increased metabolic requirements of the dam and developing conceptus. In pregnant Black Bengal goats, alterations in P-wave duration, R-wave morphology, RR interval and heart rate were observed compared with non-pregnant animals. These changes illustrate an important diagnostic principle: a deviation from the non-pregnant reference ECG does not necessarily indicate cardiovascular disease. Understanding physiological adaptation is therefore essential to avoid misinterpretation. Conversely, ECG abnormalities can provide an early indication of cardiovascular pathology. In dogs with ascites of cardiac origin, abnormalities including atrial fibrillation, irregular RR intervals, low-voltage QRS complexes, left axis deviation, ST-segment elevation and increased R-wave amplitude were observed. These findings demonstrate how systemic manifestations such as abdominal fluid accumulation can provide an indirect clue to underlying cardiovascular dysfunction. The clinical value of ECG is further illustrated by the resolution of arrhythmia in a Labrador Retriever suffering from interstitial pneumonia. Cardiac arrhythmia detected during the acute respiratory illness returned to a normal rhythm following resolution of the clinical condition. This observation highlights the dynamic interaction between the respiratory and cardiovascular systems and demonstrates that some electrical abnormalities may be secondary and reversible rather than indicative of primary structural cardiac disease. Echocardiography: linking electrical activity with cardiac structure and function Although ECG provides information primarily about electrical activity, echocardiography permits direct assessment of cardiac morphology and mechanical performance. Parameters such as left ventricular internal diameter, interventricular septal thickness, posterior wall thickness, end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, ejection fraction, fractional shortening, stroke volume, EPSS and LA/Ao ratio provide complementary information about ventricular loading, contractility and chamber dimensions. The importance of integrating ECG and echocardiography is evident in dogs presenting with different ECG abnormalities. Several ECG abnormalities were accompanied by reductions in fractional shortening and ejection fraction, suggesting that electrical disturbances may coexist with impaired mechanical performance. Tachycardia, for example, was associated with reductions in end-diastolic volume, LVIDd, ejection fraction, fractional shortening and stroke volume. Dogs with atrial fibrillation demonstrated ventricular dilation, whereas increased QRS amplitude or duration was associated with increased LA/Ao ratio. Thus, ECG abnormalities should not necessarily be interpreted as isolated electrical phenomena; they may reflect or accompany alterations in cardiac structure and haemodynamics. The relationship becomes even more apparent when cardiovascular alterations are examined in animals with apparently non-cardiac diseases. Dogs with hepatomegaly exhibited increased LVPWd, LVIDs and EPSS, together with increased heart rate, prolonged P-wave duration and a shorter PR interval. Dogs with splenomegaly demonstrated more extensive functional alterations, including increased LVIDd, EDV, LVIDs, ESV, EPSS and LA diameter, accompanied by reduced ejection fraction and fractional shortening. The simultaneous presence of electrical and mechanical alterations suggests that enlargement or dysfunction of extra-cardiac organs may be accompanied by measurable cardiovascular changes. Cardiovascular physiology in productive animals The significance of cardiovascular physiology extends beyond companion animals. In livestock, cardiovascular function is closely linked to growth, reproduction, thermoregulation and production efficiency. The heart must continuously adjust cardiac output according to physiological demand, particularly during lactation, pregnancy and exposure to environmental stress. In dairy cattle, a substantial increase in mammary blood flow is required to support milk synthesis. Approximately 500 L of blood may pass through the mammary gland for every litre of milk produced, illustrating the enormous circulatory requirement imposed by lactation. Cattle have an average stroke volume of approximately 600 mL and a heart rate of around 60 beats/min, with cardiac output reported in the range of approximately 28–52 L/min. These values demonstrate that cardiovascular function is not merely a supportive physiological process but a fundamental determinant of productive performance. Pregnancy similarly imposes substantial cardiovascular demands. Echocardiographic studies in goats have demonstrated increased left ventricular internal diameter during diastole, ejection fraction, fractional shortening, stroke volume and cardiac output during pregnancy. Cardiac output has also been reported to increase during pregnancy and lactation compared with the dry period in dairy goats. These adaptations represent physiological cardiovascular remodelling designed to meet increased tissue perfusion requirements. Therefore, comparative cardiovascular physiology provides a bridge between cardiac function and animal productivity. Changes in cardiac output, vascular resistance and myocardial performance can influence the capacity of an animal to adapt to pregnancy, lactation, exercise and environmental stress. Cardiovascular consequences of systemic disease The heart does not function independently of the rest of the organism. Alterations in hepatic, renal, respiratory or metabolic function can influence cardiovascular activity through changes in circulating volume, electrolyte balance, vascular tone, inflammatory mediators, metabolism and neuroendocrine regulation. The relationship between hepatic disease and cardiac function is particularly intriguing. Dogs with hepatic dysfunction have demonstrated abnormalities including absent P waves, tachycardia, low-voltage QRS complexes, inverted or distorted T waves and altered QRS morphology. These abnormalities were accompanied by increases in cardiac injury markers such as cardiac troponin T, LDH and CK-MB in affected groups. Similarly, dogs with hepatomegaly or splenomegaly showed alterations in both ECG and echocardiographic parameters despite the absence of overt clinical signs of primary cardiac disease. Ren

title: Radiofrequency Catheter Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation in Patients with Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return: A Multicenter Case Series
summary: ABSTRACT Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) has been observed in adults with anomalous pulmonary venous return (APVR), but data on catheter ablation outcomes in this population remain limited to case reports and small series. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 14 adult patients with confirmed APVR who underwent catheter ablation for AF at three tertiary academic centers in the United States between July 2003 and May 2025. Baseline, procedural, electroanatomic mapping, and outcome data were collected. Freedom from atrial arrhythmia recurrence was estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results Mean age was 56 ± 13 years and 79% were male. Heart failure was present in 64%, and hypertension and coronary artery disease in 43% each. Most had partial APVR (86%), and 57% had prior surgical correction. Radiofrequency ablation was used in all patients, combined with pulsed-field ablation in one. Acute success was achieved in all patients, although areas with residual pulmonary vein or SVC electrical activity were left untreated in 3 (21%). Non-pulmonary-vein electrical activity was more common in patients with prior surgical correction than in those without (43% vs 17%). Median follow-up was 3.4 years (IQR, 2.0-9.6). Freedom from arrhythmia recurrence was 78.6% at 1 year and 53.9% at 5 years. Two patients (14%) required reablation; complications occurred in 3 (21%) without long-term sequelae. Conclusions Catheter ablation was acutely successful in all patients in this largest reported APVR cohort, despite substantial comorbidity burden and anatomic complexity. The arrhythmogenic substrate often extended beyond the anomalous vein, particularly in surgically corrected patients, supporting individualized, substrate-guided ablation in this population. CLINICAL PERSPECTIVE What Is Known Atrial fibrillation has been reported in adults with anomalous pulmonary venous return (APVR), but data on catheter ablation outcomes in this population are limited to case reports and small series. What the Study Adds In the largest reported cohort of patients with APVR undergoing catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation, pulmonary vein isolation achieved acute success in all patients despite substantial comorbidity burden and anatomic complexity. Non-pulmonary-vein sites of electrical activity were more common among patients with prior surgical correction, and postsurgical scar and epicardial venoatrial connections were also arrhythmogenic, indicating that the arrhythmogenic substrate in APVR often extends beyond the anomalous vein itself. These findings support individualized, substrate-guided mapping in patients with APVR, particularly those with a surgical history, and suggest a role for pulsed-field ablation near critical structures such as the phrenic nerve.

title: Potential effect of replacing sedentary behavior with physical activity on the risk of atrial fibrillation: results from the UK Biobank and REGARDS study
summary: Background Sedentary behavior (SB) has been associated with cardiovascular disease risk, independent of physical activity (PA) and sleep. However, the effect of replacing SB with PA or sleep on atrial fibrillation (AF) risk remains unclear. Methods We studied 86,096 participants from the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB) and 5,777 from the United States (US) REasons for Geographic And Racial Differences in Stroke (REGARDS) prospective cohort studies who were free of AF at baseline and had valid accelerometry data. The two cohorts were included to evaluate the consistency of associations across distinct populations in the UK and the US, two regions with a high burden of AF. Daily time spent in light PA (LPA), moderate to vigorous PA (MVPA), and SB were derived from accelerometer recordings; sleep was accelerometer-derived in UKB and self-reported in REGARDS. Incident AF was identified using ICD-10 codes (I48.x) listed as either a primary diagnosis, secondary diagnosis, or cause of death through hospital and death registry data linkage in UKB and in a follow-up visit through electrocardiogram and self-reported medical history in REGARDS. Isotemporal substitution models were used to examine replacing 30 minutes of SB with LPA or MVPA in both cohorts and with sleep in UKB on the outcome of incident AF. Results Among the UKB participants [57% female, mean age 56.0 (SD 7.8) years, 98% White race], 4,035 AF cases were identified during a median of 7.9 years of follow-up. Replacing 30 minutes of SB with PA was associated with a slightly lower risk of AF in the minimally adjusted models but the associations were attenuated after full adjustment (LPA: HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.02; MVPA: HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.02). The REGARDS participants had an average age of 63 (SD 8.3) years, 55% female, 31% Black and 69% White adults, with 486 AF cases identified. Fully adjusted substitution of 30 minutes of SB with MVPA was associated with lower AF odds (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.63-1.01), whereas LPA showed no association. In UKB, replacing SB with sleep was not associated with AF risk. The magnitude of the association of MVPA substitution with AF appeared stronger among REGARDS participants aged ≥65 years and those reporting <7 hours/day of sleep. Conclusion Replacing SB with moderate or higher intensity PA may decrease AF risk. In REGARDS, these substitutions appeared to benefit older individuals and those reporting shorter sleep duration. These findings highlight the potential benefit of reducing sedentarism to lower AF burden, warranting validation in future studies.

title: Conductive Hydrogels as a Medium for Shapeable Catheter Ablation Electrodes
summary: ABSTRACT BACKGROUND Radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA) uses rigid metallic electrodes whose fixed geometry limits tissue contact, lesion continuity, and safe energy delivery near vulnerable structures. We evaluated a moldable, tissue-conforming conductive hydrogel as an RFCA electrode ex vivo . METHODS Poly(ether urethane diacrylamide) hydrogels with saline-tuned conductivity were molded into plugs, disks, and bars and affixed to an irrigated 8-Fr catheter. Ablations were performed on excised porcine tissue in circulated saline at 37 °C under fixed contact force and irrigation. Lesion geometry, intramural temperatures, and steam pops were compared with bare-metal (BM) electrodes and size-matched metallic analogs; an atrioesophageal stack model assessed collateral injury. Lesions were delineated using triphenyltetrazolium chloride staining. RESULTS Hydrogel bars produced wide, ellipsoidal lesions (width 10.51 ± 1.40 versus 8.71 ± 1.65 mm for BM; P =0.031; aspect ratio 1.72); size-matched metal bars produced none. Hydrogel disks produced lesions statistically indistinguishable from BM in depth (4.54 ± 0.90 versus 4.84 ± 0.55 mm) and width (9.47 ± 0.89 versus 11.41 ± 2.39 mm), whereas metal disks produced significantly shallower lesions (2.30 ± 1.70 mm; P =0.015 versus BM). In the atrioesophageal model, hydrogel plugs achieved transmural atrial lesions with a reduced esophageal lumen temperature (56.33 ± 3.80 versus 61.30 ± 5.14 °C; P =0.046), total lesion depth (4.03 ± 1.25 versus 7.58 ± 0.78 mm; P <0.001), and esophageal lesion width (3.05 ± 2.35 versus 8.70 ± 2.69 mm; P <0.001) compared with BM. Hydrogel electrodes reduced steam-pop risk (relative risk 0.34; 95% CI 0.13–0.88). Plug characterization confirmed saline-dependent conductivity and attenuated energy delivery, with lower subsurface peak temperatures and shallower lesions than BM. CONCLUSIONS Moldable, conductivity-tunable hydrogels shape RF lesions and may improve ablation safety, supporting evaluation for contiguous or linear lesion sets and ablation near sensitive structures. CLINICAL PERSPECTIVE What Is Known • Radiofrequency ablation catheters use rigid metallic electrodes, so contiguous lesion sets require sequences of closely spaced burns, and irregular tissue surfaces or thin atrial tissue near the esophagus limit uniform, safe energy delivery. • Conductive hydrogels can be molded into arbitrary shapes and tuned in electrical conductivity, but their use as a radiofrequency ablation electrode medium has not been characterized. What the Study Adds In an ex vivo porcine model, a molded hydrogel bar electrode produced wide, ellipsoidal lesions where a size-matched metal bar produced none, and a hydrogel disk produced lesions comparable to a standard bare-metal electrode where the size-matched metal disk was significantly shallower. Hydrogel electrodes attenuated energy delivery, achieving transmural atrial lesions with lower esophageal lumen temperatures, smaller esophageal lesions, and lower steam-pop risk than a bare-metal electrode. These properties support conductive hydrogel electrodes for linear lesion sets and ablation near sensitive structures, pending in vivo validation.

title: Cardiac Deceleration Capacity Refines Sudden Cardiac Death Risk Stratification in Patients with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy for Primary Prevention.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Precise sudden cardiac death risk stratification in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy remains challenging. Parasympathetic dysfunction is closely related to malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and deceleration capacity is a robust parameter to quantify vagal tone. This study aims to elucidate the association between deceleration capacity and sudden cardiac death risk in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

METHODS: A total of 648 hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients completing 24-hour ambulatory Holter monitoring were consecutively enrolled in this cohort study. Baseline deceleration capacity was calculated from the Holter recordings. The primary endpoint was a composite of sudden cardiac death or sudden-cardiac-death-equivalent events including sudden death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, and appropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapies.

RESULTS: There were 464 patients included in final analysis. During mean follow-up of 827 days, 33 (7.1%) patients met primary composite endpoint. Deceleration capacity showed a significant linear inverse association with this composite endpoint (hazard ratio 0.660 [95% confidence interval, 0.546-0.799], P < 0.001). The derived cut-off value was 6.25 ms. Adding deceleration capacity to the traditional risk model significantly improved risk discrimination (C-statistic increased from 0.732 to 0.827, Delong P = 0.019) especially in the intermediate-risk subgroup (C-statistic increased from 0.565 to 0.849, Delong P = 0.011). Patients with lower deceleration capacity and elevated risk score suffered the worst outcome (Log-rank P < 0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Deceleration capacity independently predicts sudden cardiac death risk in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and provides significant prognostic value particularly in the clinically challenging intermediate-risk subgroup. Integration of deceleration capacity into risk evaluation warrants prospective validation before guiding ICD decision-making.

title: Prognostic Impact of Left Ventricular Apical Aneurysm Identified by Echocardiography in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy ― A Multicenter Retrospective Study in Japan ―
summary: BACKGROUND: This study evaluated the prognostic impact of left ventricular (LV) apical aneurysm identified by transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in a Japanese cohort with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). METHODS AND RESULTS: We retrospectively enrolled 369 consecutive HCM patients from 2 centers (2016-2023). LV apical aneurysm was defined on TTE as a discrete, thin-walled dyskinetic/akinetic apical outpouching with a wide neck. Primary outcomes were all-cause death and cardiovascular (CV) death. Secondary outcomes were hospitalization for worsening heart failure, systemic embolism, sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), and sudden cardiac death (SCD)-equivalent events (resuscitated cardiac arrest or appropriate implantable cardioverter defibrillator therapy). LV apical aneurysm was present in 47 of 369 patients (12.7%). There were no significant between-group differences in all-cause death (log-rank P=0.162) or CV death (P=0.103). Patients with LV apical aneurysm more frequently had baseline sustained VT and SCD-equivalent events; however, Kaplan-Meier analyses indicated no significant differences between groups in incident sustained VT and SCD-equivalent events after enrollment. In multivariable Cox models, age, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and SCD-equivalent events were independently associated with all-cause death; BNP and SCD-equivalent events were independently associated with CV death. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, echocardiography-identified LV apical aneurysm was associated with a greater burden of baseline arrhythmic events, but not higher mortality. TTE provides a practical means of identifying this phenotype. BNP and SCD-equivalent events were more closely associated with mortality.

title: Potassium-Increasing Regimens in Patients at High Risk of Ventricular Arrhythmias: A Prespecified Observational Analysis of the Randomized POTCAST Trial
summary: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The POTCAST trial (n=1,200) showed that targeting high-normal plasma potassium levels reduced ventricular arrhythmias in patients with Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillators (ICDs). We compared changes in plasma potassium and described outcomes across the three regimens used to increase plasma potassium. METHODS: We studied 600 control participants and 572 intervention participants who completed potassium up-titration in POTCAST. Participants in the intervention arm were categorized according to treatment after plasma-potassium up-titration into: a) mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists (MRAs) monotherapy, b) potassium-supplement monotherapy, or c) combination-therapy with both. The primary endpoint was a composite of sustained ventricular arrhythmia, appropriate ICD-therapy, hospitalization for arrhythmia or heart-failure or all-cause mortality. Safety outcomes included death and electrolyte/renal disturbances. RESULTS: After six months, plasma potassium increased from 4.12 to 4.27 mmol/L (p=0.004) with MRA, from 3.99 to 4.24 mmol/L (p<0.001) with potassium-supplements, and from 3.98 to 4.34 mmol/L (p<0.001) with combination-therapy. The primary endpoint occurred in 29% (n=175) of controls, 22% (n=16) in the MRA group, 21% (n=31) in the potassium-supplements group and in 22% (n=72) in the combination-therapy group (p=0.8 between regimens). Hypokalemia occurred in 13% of controls and in 3%, 9%, and 5% of participants receiving MRA, potassium-supplements and combination-therapy, respectively. Hyperkalemia occurred in 0.2% of controls and in 0%, 3%, and 4% of participants receiving MRA, potassium-supplements, and combination-therapy (p>0.1 between regimens). CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with MRA, potassium-supplements or both increased potassium levels. All regimens were associated with numerically lower endpoint rates than controls. We detected no statistically significant differences in endpoints or safety between regimens.

title: Artificial intelligence and remote monitoring of cardiac devices: A narrative review.
summary: Remote monitoring of Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices (CIEDs) has evolved significantly from early trans-telephonic transmissions to now becoming a standard of care that improves survival and outcomes. However, the resulting exponential growth in data has resulted in alert fatigue and information overload, creating a need for advanced data interpretation. This narrative review examines the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in reshaping remote monitoring and cardiac device management into an active, predictive, and personalised system. We examine the role of AI across all cardiac implantable electronic devices, including implantable loop recorders (ILRs), pacemakers, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) and cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) devices. We address four questions: (1) the scale and nature of the remote monitoring burden; (2) the AI tools in current clinical use, particularly for ILRs, where alert burden is greatest; (3) AI applications evaluated but not yet widely implemented, including prediction of ventricular arrhythmias, heart failure events and device failure; and (4) future directions, including adaptive device programming and digital twins. While AI demonstrates significant potential to enhance clinical decision-making and patient outcomes, its widespread adoption remains constrained by barriers regarding data quality, algorithm transparency, regulatory compliance, and privacy protections. Realising the full potential of AI in electrophysiology will require sustained collaboration between clinical and technical stakeholders to ensure these tools are deployed effectively and safely.

title: Cardiac warning symptoms in paediatric out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest survivors.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in children is a rare but devastating event, with an estimated incidence of 9 per 100 000 person-years and a survival rate of less than 10%. OHCA may be the presenting event in children with undiagnosed cardiovascular disease. A substantial proportion of adults experiencing an unexpected OHCA report previous symptoms, but whether the same is true in paediatric survivors has not been systematically evaluated previously. This study aims to describe cardiac symptoms in children prior to presenting with OHCA.

METHODS: Clinical characteristics and preceding symptoms of 58 consecutive patients aged 0-18 without a pre-existing causative diagnosis presenting with a survived OHCA between 1996 and 2025 to a single UK paediatric tertiary referral centre were reviewed.

RESULTS: The median age at cardiac arrest was 11 years (IQR 7-14 years). 29 OHCA (50%) occurred on exertion. Following the OHCA, 42 patients (72.4%) were diagnosed with an inherited cardiac condition, most commonly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (n=17, 29.8%). 18 patients (31.0%) had a family history of sudden cardiac death.28 patients (50.9%) had reported cardiac symptoms prior to their OHCA, including 13 (23.6%) who had experienced syncope. Of the 13 patients who experienced syncope, only three sought medical attention and none had follow-up arranged.

CONCLUSIONS: Almost half of paediatric OHCA survivors had warning symptoms prior to their event, representing potential missed opportunities to identify an underlying diagnosis prior to OHCA. These findings highlight the need for more education, both for medical professionals and the general public, about 'red flag' symptoms.

title: Rhythm and conduction disorders in children with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
summary: Rhythm and conduction disorders remain key determinants of prognosis in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Objective. To assess the nature, frequency, and clinical-prognostic significance of cardiac rhythm and conduction disorders in children with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Materials and Methods . This retrospective-prospective study included 200 children with confirmed primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (median age 14.34 years; 2/3 male). Median follow-up was 5.74 years. Life-threatening arrhythmias were defined as sudden cardiac death, aborted sudden cardiac death, or appropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy. Results. Rhythm and conduction disorders were detected in 77 % of children. Ventricular extrasystole ≥ 10/24h was observed in 25.5 %, and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia in 20.5 %. Life-threatening arrhythmias occurred in 27 children (13.5 %): sudden cardiac death (n = 6), aborted sudden cardiac death (n = 11), and appropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator shocks for primary prevention (n = 10). Ventricular extrasystole 10–500/24h (OR 4.93; p = 0.00002) and ventricular extrasystole ≥ 500/24h (OR 6.84; p = 0.015) were associated with non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Extreme myocardial hypertrophy increased the odds of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia 2.3-fold (p = 0.018). Sick sinus syndrome was diagnosed in 10.5 % of children and was a strong predictor of life-threatening arrhythmias (OR 5.18; p<0.001). Intraventricular conduction disturbances were noted in 54.5 %, first-degree atrioventricular block in 20 %, and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias in 5.5 %. Conclusion . Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by a high prevalence of rhythm and conduction disorders. Even moderate ventricular extrasystole is associated with non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, justifying routine Holter monitoring in all children with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sick sinus syndrome is associated with a fivefold increased risk of life-threatening arrhythmias and should be incorporated into sudden cardiac death risk stratification algorithms. Such patients may warrant a lower 5-year sudden cardiac death risk threshold for dual-chamber cardioverter-defibrillator implantation.

Comparison of the Effects of Diazepam, Acepromazine and Xylazine as Preanesthetic Agents in Preventing Cardiac Arrhythmias in Sheep Under General Anesthesia with Ketamine
summary: Abstract Cardiac arrhythmias are an important potential complication of general anesthesia. This dissertation investigated and compared the effects of the preanesthetic agents diazepam, acepromazine, and xylazine on the occurrence of cardiac arrhythmias in sheep anesthetized with ketamine. The study used electrocardiographic monitoring to evaluate cardiac responses during anesthesia and examined the susceptibility of the animals to epinephrine-induced ventricular arrhythmias. The preanesthetic agents were compared under controlled experimental conditions, with particular attention to the dose of epinephrine required to provoke clinically significant ventricular ectopic activity. The results indicated that the three preanesthetic drugs did not provide a uniform or reliable protective effect against epinephrine-induced cardiac arrhythmias during ketamine anesthesia. The findings emphasize the importance of careful cardiovascular monitoring when ketamine anesthesia is used in sheep, particularly when sympathetic stimulation or catecholamine administration may occur.
